writing.exampleCaption: One syscall per line, versus one per buffer.
writing.explanation:
Reading a file, opening a socket, or spawning a thread all cross a privilege boundary that costs far more than a function call. That is why buffering and batching can help when per-call overhead matters, while event loops can handle many mostly idle connections efficiently. Interviewers ask this to see whether you know where the cost of IO actually is.

A system call crosses from user code into the kernel to request a privileged operation. The transition and work on the other side have cost, but there is no single fixed ratio to a function call: data size, caching, contention, device latency, and kernel path all matter. Buffered I/O can combine many small writes into fewer requests. Scatter/gather I/O can send several buffers in one call. Batching is valuable when per-call overhead is a measurable part of the workload, not as a rule to apply blindly.

An event loop uses readiness or completion notifications so a thread need not block separately on every mostly idle connection. `epoll` and `io_uring` expose different Linux models, but neither guarantees superiority for every operation. A simple blocking read may be the best choice for a small tool. In Rust, a crate's API may buffer or batch internally, so profile the actual program before assuming the source line maps to one syscall.

In an interview, describe one concrete path: a program calls write, the kernel validates the request and copies or references data according to the API, then the call returns a result that may be partial or an error. Explain why a loop must handle short writes. If the question is performance, propose a measurement: syscall count, bytes per call, time waiting on I/O, and tail latency. The answer should connect the kernel boundary to the observed workload, not just name a fashionable interface.

Batching introduces a latency tradeoff: waiting to accumulate a large buffer can delay one small urgent write. Set a flush policy based on payload size or time budget. Partial I/O remains possible even after batching, so the loop must track bytes completed and retry the rest without duplicating already-sent data.
writing.feedback: The boundary crossing dominates; batch before you optimise anything else.
